body:
Parashat Nitzavim

This week’s parashah opens with a vivid scene:

“You are all standing today before Hashem your God—your heads, your tribes, your elders, your officers, every man of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and the stranger in your camp—from the wood-chopper to the water-drawer—to enter into the covenant of Hashem your God.” (Deut. 29:9-11)

From the highest leader to the person drawing water, every soul is present. No one is too lofty to be included, and no one is too small to matter. Hashem renews the covenant as we prepare to enter the Land, reminding us that this relationship is not only national but deeply personal.

“Why Am I Responsible?”

Many of us quietly ask this question. I’m one person. Why must my choices, my actions, carry weight for the whole? Rabbi Gerzi teaches that Jews are doers—diggers of wells. We are not meant to let the world simply happen to us; we are called to happen to the world, to carve out spaces of holiness and life-giving water wherever we stand. The covenant demands that each of us become an active participant. From the above statement of this parsha and what we learn from our Rebbi is that I am responsible, I am a doer, not just a passive observer.

Who are we responsible for and the silent tochacha

Chazal teach, “Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh—all of Israel are guarantors for one another” (Shevuot 39a). Responsibility isn’t abstract. The Torah continues, “The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever, to do all the words of this Torah” (Devarim 29:28). We are not judged for what is truly hidden, but once wrongdoing becomes public—or once we have the ability to guide someone—we share in the duty to act.

The mitzvah of tochachah (rebuke) gives this responsibility a practical framework: “You shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him” (Vayikra 19:17). Chazal (Arakhin 16b) teach that true rebuke must be gentle and constructive, aimed at helping, not humiliating. If I know how to speak in a way that might reach someone, I am obligated to try. But tochachah is more than words. The Rambam notes that living with integrity—showing kindness, honesty, and faithfulness—is itself a silent rebuke and a model for others. How I carry myself “in the street,” a is often the strongest tochachah of all. Simply by acting with dignity, responsibility and even safety like wearing a bicycle helmet to show the importance, I help lift the people around me.

Hidden and Revealed

Nitzavim acknowledges the limits of our reach:

“The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever, to fulfill all the words of this Torah.” (Deut. 29:28)

If someone secretly hides an idol under the bed, that is for God alone to judge. But when wrongdoing becomes public—when it shapes the moral texture of the community—the responsibility becomes ours. The Talmud teaches, Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh—all Israel are guarantors for one another (Shavuot 39a). Blessings and curses are addressed to the entire nation because covenantal life is shared life.

We see this principle in the story of Rachel hiding her father Lavan’s teraphim (Gen. 31). Jacob cannot be punished for what he does not know. Only the one who acts in secret faces that private judgment. But once sin is visible, silence is complicity.

Integrity of the Heart

The Torah calls us to a wholeness that spans private and public. Shiviti Hashem lenegdi tamid—“I place Hashem before me always” (Ps. 16:8). Whether people are watching or not, our lives must reflect God’s presence. Our private selves must match the image we project in the synagogue, the workplace, or the street. Rambam (Hilchot De’ot 6:7) frames this as a mitzvah of tochachah—offering gentle, constructive guidance—because only a community of integrity can sustain the covenant.

Growth That Flows Outward

Personal growth in Torah is never only for self-perfection, it’s about us growing to help others and growing with others as well. We refine ourselves so that we can lift others. Study turns into prayer; prayer flows into acts of tzedakah. As we approach Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, we repeat: Teshuvah, Tefillah, Tzedakah—repentance, prayer, and righteous giving—ma’avirin et ro’a hagezeirah, can sweeten even a harsh decree. The flow of this is like what we have been working on throughout all of Devarim,

First we turn inward with teshuva, a self reflection to own what I am responsible for and to make that right.

Then we speak upward, I ask Hashem to help me to make right between me and others and me and Him.

Finally we act outward with tzedaka, where my physical mitzvot impact those around me in a way where I can help, show and elevate. Each step strengthens the covenant we all share.

The Answer

So why am I responsible? Because covenant is not a contract with the crowd; it is a marriage between God and each of us, renewed in every generation. Hashem addresses kulchem—“all of you”—but also le’ovrecha—“that you may pass into the covenant” (Deut. 29:11), in the singular. The nation stands as one body, yet every individual is a vital organ. If even one part fails, the whole is diminished.

My responsibility is not a burden but a calling: to be the well-digger, the light-bearer, the person whose private faith and public action invite blessing to the entire community.

Atem nitzavim hayom kulchem—we stand today, all of us, together. And because we stand together, my choices matter. My growth protects others, my prayer lifts others, my tzedakah sustains others. I am responsible because I am indispensable.

May our personal teshuvah and our shared responsibility join to bring renewal and peace to all Israel and the world in the year ahead.

Parshat Nitzavim – Standing Together, Bearing Responsibility

This week’s parsha opens with a powerful scene: “You are all standing today before Hashem your God – your leaders, tribes, elders, officers, every person in Israel” (Devarim 29:9). The Torah goes out of its way to list every group. Rashi explains that this gathering took place on the day of Moshe’s death, binding the entire nation—leaders and water-carriers alike—into one covenant. It’s not just a historic moment; it’s a call to collective responsibility.

Chazal teach, “Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh—all of Israel are guarantors for one another” (Shevuot 39a). Responsibility isn’t abstract. The Torah continues, “The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever, to do all the words of this Torah” (Devarim 29:28). We are not judged for what is truly hidden, but once wrongdoing becomes public—or once we have the ability to guide someone—we share in the duty to act.

The mitzvah of tochachah (rebuke) gives this responsibility a practical framework: “You shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him” (Vayikra 19:17). Chazal (Arakhin 16b) teach that true rebuke must be gentle and constructive, aimed at helping, not humiliating. If I know how to speak in a way that might reach someone, I am obligated to try. But tochachah is more than words. The Rambam notes that living with integrity—showing kindness, honesty, and faithfulness—is itself a silent rebuke and a model for others. How I carry myself “in the street,” as Rabbi Gerzi once taught, is often the strongest tochachah of all. Simply by acting with dignity and responsibility, I help lift the people around me.

This idea echoes through the season of the Yamim Nora’im. On Rosh Hashanah we all stand together in judgment, just as we stood together in the covenant of Nitzavim. Our actions influence not only our own verdict but the spiritual climate of our community.

Consider the episode of Yaakov and Rachel (Bereishit 31). Rachel hid her father’s idols, and Yaakov, unaware, declared that whoever had taken them would die. Though Rachel’s act was hidden even from Yaakov, the Sages explain that his words opened a gate of judgment and shortened her life. The hidden was ultimately revealed. It’s a sobering reminder: the lines between private and public, between my responsibility and another’s, are more porous than we imagine.

All of this circles back to our parsha’s opening: “You are all standing today.” We are bound together. When I know how to guide someone and hold back, I fail them. When I live carelessly, I teach carelessness. But when I choose integrity, I give natural tochachah—quiet leadership that can awaken others. As Rabbi Gerzi puts it, “Your life speaks even when you are silent.”

That is why I am responsible: because covenant means community, and community means that my choices—seen and unseen—shape the spiritual reality we all share.
